IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00853

But fitting these traditions into such a scheme is far from straightforward. Mr Coyajee nevertheless believes that if we agree to identify the eight Kayanids, guardians of the Xvarnah, with the sacred Lineage of the Grail, all the difficulties posed by different versions of the family relationship between the Grail's guardian and the knight who completes the Quest disappear. The desolation of the Grail Domain can then be explained by the murder of Siyavakhsh, son of Kay Kâûs and bearer of the Xvarnah, treacherously killed by Afrasiyab the Turanian, whose son-in-law he had become. Ultimately Kay Khosraw and Parsifal shine through one another as heroes who win, or win back, the Xvarnah or the Grail.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00854

The consequence of such a proposal would be to derive the Arthurian epic of the Grail directly and entirely from the Iranian epic of the Xvarnah, as from the source with which it must therefore have been identical at the beginning.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00855

Perhaps this proposal is too quickly satisfied with outward, material facts, as though we were tracing the antecedents of Corneille's Le Cid among its Spanish predecessors, or showing that one Gallic tribe descended from another. That is why, from the phenomenologist's standpoint, the proposal seems at once to go too far and yet to stop short of the real issue. It goes too far because its claim of actual historical identity is extremely vulnerable; and in defending that claim we risk losing everything we have gained from the parallels themselves.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00856

Yet in doing so it still stops short of what those parallels imply: they allow us to glimpse an entire sphere of spirituality shared by the idea of the Xvarnah and the idea of the Grail. It is one thing to say that the Kayanids stand in relation to the Xvarnah as the sacred Lineage does to the Grail. It is quite another to say that the second lineage is historically identical with the first. To doubt this material identification is in no way to abandon the parallels already discerned.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00857

Rather, we must bring out their full significance in the way Suhrawardi himself would have done: by understanding the kind of bond he establishes between the Khosrawâniyûn, the sages of divine wisdom in ancient Persia, and the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of light in Islamic Iran. The historian, who can pronounce only on material facts, naturally shakes his head at something that escapes the categories of empirical science and cannot be explained by tracing one instance of the same thing back to another.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00858

When a philosopher recognizes his spiritual ancestors and claims descent from them, however, this is not a succession of legal heirs whose rights can be established by archival documents. It is an innovating event, one that takes place in the history of the soul. Its effects can reach backward into that soul's past and reshape it, so that the event cannot be “explained” merely by reducing it to an earlier occurrence. Or rather, its true “antecedent” lies elsewhere, on the level of a world of which historical reality here below is only a passing manifestation.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00859

One thing shared by the Kayanid dynasty and the dynasty of the Grail is that both escape the chronological classifications of our history books. Attempts to identify the Kayanids with the Achaemenids known to the Greeks have failed. Here, then, is a lineage of heroes whose deeds and attributes are distinct and whose tradition continues from the Avesta to the Shâh-Nâmeh, yet to whom we cannot assign dates. (The same is true of Zoroaster, for whom the various proposed dates remain approximations.) The Kayanids enter history only through the resonant invocation of the hymn that celebrates them or the epic that tells their story.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00860

And yet the events of their epic are perfectly real—real in a dimension different from that of the history Julius Caesar recounts, for example, in his Commentaries. That is why we prefer to speak not of a “mythical prehistory” but of an archehistory: a history of origins that stands in relation to ordinary history as an archetype stands to its particular expression.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00861

Likewise, the Grail lineage enters history only as the light of a sanctuary shines through a stained-glass window into the darkness outside. What common measure could there be between that light and Caesar's Commentaries? But rather than diminish the claim, let us say that the sacred history of the Grail is projected onto the historical scene as nothing less than such a light—and cannot even be fixed in place there, since nothing on that scene foretold its coming or offers a measure for it.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00862

The lineage of the Holy Grail has no place in official Church history. It does not even compete with the succession to the Apostolic See; it simply knows nothing of it. Instead of Peter or James, it speaks of Joseph of Arimathea and the mysterious Josephé. References to the Norman-Angevin Plantagenet dynasty in certain works of the Grail cycle belong to the transformation of Glastonbury, Arthur's sanctuary, into a holy place. Within that transformation lived the aspirations of a Celtic Church that had earlier been abolished by force, now rising again as a secret Church of the Grail, to endure incognito in this world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00863

How many other facts lead us directly into a history that is metahistory, and therefore also archehistory! We might also compare the transmission of the Light of Glory from Ohrmazd's heaven to Kay Khosraw with the transmission of the “Muhammadan Light” (Nûr mohammadî), created at the beginning of all things: from the heavenly Adam through prophet after prophet to Muhammad, and from Imam to Imam until the Twelfth.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00864

The lineage of the Twelve Imams does not compete with some worldly dynasty on the same plane. As we have already observed, it is the esoteric line that guards the “Muhammadan Light” and the walâyat, the spiritual authority and bond of devotion; from the beginning, the number of these “upholders” was fixed in advance at twelve. Its concern is something quite different from what people today call “doing history.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00865

With all this in mind, what do we mean when we speak of a “meeting” between the Iranian chivalry of the Xvarnah and the Celtic chivalry of the Grail? Is it a fact that can be “explained,” causally deduced, because Druids and Magi may have met in Asia Minor, or Druids and initiates of Mithraic mysteries in Celtic lands and Britain? We need not even mention the scarcity of documents on the matter. The essential point is simply this: Druids and Magi, Druids and Mithraic initiates, could have stood side by side for centuries, and the meeting we are concerned with might never have taken place.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00866

Indeed, why should there not have been hostility, reserve, or rivalry? If a researcher with “open eyes” can now discern the event of this meeting, it matters that the researcher discern where the event took place, and at what level of knowledge and plane of being it has meaning.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00867

In the same way, the Gospel of Nicodemus, containing the sacred history of Joseph of Arimathea, and the entire Celtic saga of King Arthur and his Round Table could have coexisted materially in the Western world—in libraries, for instance—without a single knight ever setting out on the Quest for the Grail revealed at the Last Supper, and hidden from the world again since Galahad's ecstatic death. For that quest to begin, the event of their meeting had to occur. Where, and how? Precisely where the Gospel of Nicodemus ceased to be an “apocryphal” book and became a book brought fully into the light.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00868

Suhrawardi speaks to us of events that take place: that is, events that have their place in the Malakût. A spiritual event indeed “happens” somewhere other than in social history, literary history, the history of ideas, and so on. In certain periods, this is perhaps the hardest kind of event to imagine or grasp—if it can be grasped at all.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00869

We shall have reason to return to this when discussing the idea of hikâyat, or mystical narrative. There is no history of a particular spirituality other than that spirituality itself, alive and at work. Otherwise it is no longer its history. We meet again the situation we encountered in the preceding book when trying to understand the events of Shiism. The dilemma was already before us: either acknowledge that some events belong to a history different from the one examined by empirical science, or impose upon them from outside categories that are not their own. In the latter case, the events elude us at the very moment we think we have grasped them.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00870

By contrast, the researcher who has somehow become capable of “receiving” these events, having adjusted the powers of perception to their true nature, has much to learn from the parallel Mr Coyajee draws between the deeds of Kay Khosraw and those of Parsifal. We have just as much to learn when Suhrawardi claims Kay Khosraw—the figure from whom the mystical sages called Khosrawâniyûn take their name—as a spiritual ancestor of his Ishrâqîyûn. What Kay Khosraw's saga teaches us about the ecstatic sovereign already prepares the way for the spiritual lineage formed within the Malakût, the setting of every event in sacred history. For we can never be mere spectators of such events.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00871

Suhrawardi himself becomes an active witness to them, as he does in his psalms and mystical tales. He can do so because his entire spirituality is eschatological—concerned with the ultimate destiny of existence—just as Kay Khosraw, King Arthur, and Parsifal are figures of that destiny, and just as the meaning of the “Orient,” of the “return to the Orient,” is eschatological. It means becoming hidden from the world of sensory appearances, in a quest that can be completed only beyond this world, in the universes upon which the very appearance of this world depends. This is why Suhrawardi's tales mark, above all, the passage from the Iranian heroic epic to the mystical epic.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
en-book-2-ch-4-s3
3. Kay Khosraw and Parsifal
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00872

Even the brief comparison we have sketched will help bring into focus the prince to whom Suhrawardi, in agreement with tradition, assigns an exceptional place among the sages of ancient Persia: Kay Khosraw, son of Siyavakhsh and Ferangiz, the daughter of Afrasiyab the Turanian.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00873

Every text celebrates him as an extraordinary man, and Zoroastrian tradition honours him as one who understood and practised the Mazdaean religion even before Zoroaster's prophetic mission. He was the eighth and last sovereign of the Kayanid line, king of Xvaniratha: the central keshvar, or clime, of the seven regions that make up the Mazdaean Imago Terrae, the spiritual image of the earth. He is “one of the seven immortal princes of Xvaniratha”—one of those who, now withdrawn to a refuge invisible to the inhabitants of this world, will accompany the Saoshyant, together with some of their knights, when he prepares the transfiguration of the world (frashkart) at the end of our Aeon. This same theme reappears in Twelver Shiism in the companions of the Twelfth Imam.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00874

We have noted this already, and shall have occasion to recall it again, for the entire spirit of Iranian religious life seems to vibrate to the same underlying note. Kay Khosraw's person, his role, and his epic are eschatological through and through: his story continues and reaches its end in a world beyond ours, at once very close and very far away.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00875

An essential feature of this vision of the last things is the mystical fortress. Its location cannot be plotted on any map, and it invites certain comparisons with the castle of the Grail. It remains on the horizon throughout the tragedies in which the fates of Kay Khosraw's grandfather and father—Kay Kâûs and Siyavakhsh—are bound together. In the end, it becomes the hidden place where Kay Khosraw's own exaltation reaches fulfilment.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00876

Having completed his mission and his reign, Kay Khosraw withdraws to the mystical castle of Kang-Dêz. To withdraw there is to become hidden from the eyes of this world. A few heroes and prophets have entered it without first crossing the threshold of death. That is what the final scene—one of the most beautiful in Ferdowsi's Shâh-Nâmeh—will show us.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00877

The fortress of Kang-Dêz belongs to the theme of the Mysterious Dwellings built by kings and heroes, whose significance for the destiny of the world is fundamental. Where is this mysterious castle? People have sought it sometimes in the east, sometimes in the far north. All these locations can be true, because particular geographical places correspond to particular visionary experiences.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00878

But to verify those experiences, we must leave our maps behind. The far north is the celestial Pole, the “Emerald Rock,” and there, as Suhrawardi knows, the “intermediate Orient” begins. Whether the castle is said to stand in the heart or on the summit of Mount Alborz, or of Mount Qâf, the meaning is the same: it belongs to the “eighth clime.” To reach it, one must pass through the centre of the central clime, through Erân-Vêj in medio mundi, at the world's centre. We thus have the two poles of the axis joining soul and cosmos.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00879

Perhaps the best indication, then, is the one tradition itself gives us: “On the border of Erân-Vêj.” It is precisely at that “border” that the hero's destiny and that of his fortress are decided. This is why the castle has so many counterparts. There is the var, the enclosed refuge of Yima (Jamshid), which generates its own light. Within it, the chosen preserve eternal youth so that, after the world's destruction, they may one day repopulate it with a higher humanity. Kay Kâûs builds his own castle on the same model.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00880

But Yima and Kay Kâûs are “wounded” sovereigns, made “mortal” through their own fault. It will fall to Kay Khosraw to establish the fortress securely and withdraw into it to await the appointed time. There are also the dwellings of the powers of Darkness: Afrasiyab's underground stronghold, for example, where he is protected by an iron enclosure. We are greatly simplifying this whole account. What chiefly concerns us is the contrast it presents, parallel to that between the Grail castle and the evil castle of the magician Klingschor (Klingsor), the “Castle of Wonders.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00881

The fortress of Kay Kâûs, Kay Khosraw's grandfather, is also the scene of his own tragedy. At the heart or summit of Alborz—that is, of Mount Qâf (the place to which Suhrawardi's mystical tales likewise lead us back)—Kay Kâûs, still sovereign of the seven keshvars, has an immense palace built with seven dwellings: one of gold, two of silver, two of steel, and two of crystal.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00882

From this fortress he holds at bay all the demons Ahriman has unleashed upon the world. The seven palaces have a magical virtue: if a person weakened by age and threatened by approaching death enters through one gate of the enclosure, that person comes out through the other looking like a fifteen-year-old youth. Kay Kâûs himself had undergone this transformation. Its symbolic meaning is transparent, like everything associated with the approaches to the “Source of Life.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00883

But then Kay Kâûs is seized by the dizzying desire for power. For at this “border” a human being faces a choice: either understand that the only passage beyond it is the way Kay Khosraw will take, or imagine that weapons and machines can still be of some use. This is the tragic mistake: what kind of “heavenly” space are we speaking of? The world of Light is not a world one can enter with machines and weapons, however “modern” they may be.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00884

Yet Kay Kâûs's mistake has been repeated down to our own day. And now Kay Kâûs, at the head of an army made up of the very demons he once fought, assaults heaven. Of course he cannot cross the boundary between Darkness and heavenly Light—that is, he cannot escape the world of becoming and death. His army perishes; he falls back to earth, wounded forever and deprived of his Xvarnah. In later traditions, such as Ferdowsi's, the flying device—already familiar from an episode of the Greek Romance of Alexander—is absurd but no less significant: a basket carried aloft by eagles, enticed by pieces of meat hung from the lances to which the birds are fastened.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00885

However high he had risen, Kay Kâûs had never truly left this world. Now wounded and powerless before the demon of death, he can only await the one whom the Xvarnah—or the Grail—will make a victorious hero.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00886

From this moment the victorious hero enters “history,” but a history whose true setting is the Malakût. We do not know at what date in our historical chronology Zoroaster entered this world. We are told, however, by the Dênkart, that his Fravarti—his heavenly being—was created at the beginning of the fourth “millennium” of our Aeon in the spiritual world, the world in its mênôk state.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00887

In the same way, we learn here that, after Kay Kâûs's defeat, as he flees, he is pursued by Neryoseng, “messenger of the gods, promoter of the worlds,” who wishes to finish him off. Neryoseng is prevented from doing so by the Fravarti of Kay Khosraw: the heavenly being who exists before Kay Khosraw's earthly birth, his archetypal self of light, his “angel.” Kay Khosraw's Fravarti intercedes because it knows that Kay Kâûs must live to father Siyavakhsh, so that it—the Fravarti—may itself enter this world and fulfil its mission as the hero who defeats Afrasiyab and the powers of Darkness.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00888
Hence the terms in which Kay Khosraw's Fravarti is invoked in a hymn of the Avesta.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00889

After Kay Kâûs's failure, his son Siyavakhsh in turn builds the mystical fortress that will be called Kang-Dêz, in the far north, amid the highest mountains: in other words, at the heart or summit of the cosmic mountain.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00890

But although Siyavakhsh begins the work, only Kay Khosraw will “stabilize” the fortress and give it its lasting order. Kang-Dêz is marked by two features: its astonishing architecture, that of a city in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world; and its role in the final destiny of the world. The fortress has seven walls, made respectively of gold, silver, steel, bronze, iron, crystal, and precious stone. Within its enclosure rise fourteen mountains; seven navigable rivers flow through it. The land is so fertile that grass grows to the height of a man in a single night.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00891

There are fifteen gates, each as tall as fifty men. The diagonal distance from one gate to another is seven hundred parasangs, a journey of twenty-two days in spring or fifteen days in summer. In this city—whose description resembles those of Jâbarsâ, Jâbalqâ, and Hûrqalyâ in the “eighth clime”—dwells Khôrshêd-Tchehr, one of Zoroaster's sons. He will lead the companions of Peshotûn, the city's ruler and another hero of the last days, son of King Vishtaspa, Zoroaster's protector, in the final battle against the powers of Ahriman. This is where Kay Khosraw has withdrawn as one of the seven princes who will accompany the future Saoshyant.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00892

The inhabitants of Kang-Dêz are described in the same terms as those of Hûrqalyâ in Suhrawardi's writings: happy and glorious, faithful and devout, strangers to old age and death. (Compare below, Book VII, the inhabitants of the Green Island, home of the Hidden Imam.) They will return to the land of Iran, to Erânshahr, only to prepare the transfiguration of the world (frashkart) through the victory of Ohrmazd and the Amahraspands and the destruction of Ahriman.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00893

But between the moment when Kay Khosraw's Fravarti interceded for Kay Kâûs and the moment when Kay Khosraw, having fulfilled his mission on earth, left this world for the mysterious fortress, a long tragedy unfolds. It is a family tragedy that drives Prince Siyavakhsh into exile; and, paradoxically, he finds refuge with the eternal enemy, Afrasiyab. He marries Afrasiyab's daughter Ferangiz. For a moment there seems to be a premonition that Afrasiyab might be redeemed through his daughter.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00894

Yet Afrasiyab falls prey to intrigue and treacherously orders Siyavakhsh's death. The young woman, now pregnant, is saved by the wisdom of a great Turanian dignitary. It takes a dream vision, an unexpected consent, and a daring, perilous flight for mother and child to set out secretly for distant Iran. They will be found, in the solitude of forests and mountains, by a band of Iranian knights—led by the valiant Giv—who have been searching for the guardian and bearer of the Xvarnah for seven years.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00895

Thus begins the chapter we might call “The Childhood of Kay Khosraw,” which Mr Coyajee has compared with “The Childhood of Parsifal.” The son of Siyavakhsh and the son of Gahmuret have each lost his father through treachery and betrayal. Each has a princess for his mother; each is raised by her in the solitude of forests and mountains; each learns from her the secret of his origins, unknown to everyone else. Both spend their childhood in the woods, playing at being knights. When they first appear at a royal court, they astonish everyone with their ignorance of courtly manners. Both are “sons of a pure heart.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00896

Just as Parsifal comes to the court of the Fisher King, Kay Khosraw comes to that of his grandfather, King Kay Kâûs, himself a “wounded” king who lies waiting for the one who will guard the Xvarnah. Both have the same duty to set right a wrong: Kay Khosraw must avenge his father Siyavakhsh against the violator of the Xvarnah; Parsifal must defeat the Fisher King's enemy and avenge the death of his brother Goon. Both will restore the king's health, free the land from its magical prohibition, and bring spring bursting forth again. One will become sovereign through the royal Xvarnah; the other, king of the Grail.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00897

According to the epic tradition, Kay Khosraw's heroic deeds begin with the episode already described: the collapse of the evil, enchanted fortress under the blow of his supernatural lance, and the appearance of the paradisal Dwelling. Religious tradition speaks instead of the destruction of a temple of idols.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00898

In either case, it is not the light of an ordinary physical flame that disperses the Darkness gathered by demons before Kay Khosraw. It is one of the three forms of Fire corresponding to the three manifestations of the Xvarnah: Adhar Gushasp, the Fire of kings and knights. This royal Fire settles upon his horse's mane and drives away the darkness produced by the enchantments, enabling Kay Khosraw to make out the idol temple and destroy it. In its place he builds a temple to the royal Fire. This temple has been located in Azerbaijan, on the shores of Lake Urmia or on Mount Savalan, where Zoroaster's conversations with Ohrmazd and his archangels have also been located.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00899

We have already discussed how the westward movement of the Zoroastrian Magi consecrated the “visionary calling” of certain geographical places. The faculty that perceives the holiness of places and knows that particular events “took place” there is a malakûti faculty: a faculty of the spiritual world, not one of empirical perception. An ancient tradition aptly reminds us that the sacred places of the Mazdaean Imago Terrae cannot be seen by ordinary eyes: “Kay Khosraw,” we are told, “concealed the entrance to the temple he had dedicated to the royal Fire, so that no one, until the Day of Resurrection, knows where the temple stands.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00900

Surely it is also along the horizons of a geography beyond the senses—a “geosophy,” or wisdom of sacred places—that we must follow Kay Khosraw's quest: the extraordinary, far-ranging journeys that occupy seven years as he pursues Afrasiyab-Ahriman to destroy him. The journey extends as far as the Sphere of the Stars. Some of these regions can be identified on our maps, but many others certainly cannot. The entire route is marked chiefly by landmarks through which a long tradition suggests the soul's struggles—the struggles that “take place” in the Malakût: crossings of deserts, mysterious voyages over distant seas, and the like.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00901

Kay Khosraw crosses Khotan and travels as far as China, then to the remote coast of Makran. There he embarks upon a mysterious sea and, after seven months' sailing, reaches Afrasiyab's fortress, the underground Kang-Dêz. He captures it and destroys it, along with its ruler. Once the one who tried to seize the Xvarnah by force has been destroyed, the task is complete, and the return to Iran retraces the journey in reverse. This journey still takes place in the dimension where two opposed poles face one another: Afrasiyab's underground fortress and Kay Khosraw's paradisal Kang-Dêz.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00902

The hero cannot enter the latter until he has destroyed its opposite, its shadow. He must draw inward and pass through all the climes of the world and the soul before standing “on the border of Erân-Vêj,” in medio mundi—at the centre of the world—and there entering the centre that is also the origin, the “Land of Visions,” where the laws of the physical world cease to rule. The search for the “Source of Life” stretches across all the climes before leading back to the centre. It is the same direction the “archangel of fire” will show the ishrâqî pilgrim, who reaches his goal only at the end of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00903

From the moment the Light of Glory rests upon Kay Khosraw—as the kingship of the Grail rests upon Parsifal—everything has been accomplished. The years during which their reigns continue on earth change nothing essential; the spiritual impulse simply becomes more clearly defined. The hero is already a figure of the final destiny of the world, destined to bring the heroic epic to completion as a mystical epic. The latter will be fulfilled in the “Land of Visions,” in that “Orient” where the blessed Kay Khosraw was carried into the presence of the “Wisdom (Sophia) of the Most Holy Father.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00904

Suhrawardi expressly referred to this vision more than once to show that the “Oriental” philosophers of divine wisdom, the ishrâqîyûn, were none other than the khosrawâniyûn of ancient Persia, whose name derives from Kay Khosraw. In the eyes of this world, King Kay Khosraw is moving toward occultation—concealment from ordinary sight, in the sense used in Shiism of the occultation of the Twelfth Imam.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00905

The physical laws governing his presence in this world are suspended, for the relationship between the “eighth clime” and the other seven climes is not governed by physics. The “eighth clime” is at once very near and very far. This is why such a presence—in the sense of final, awaited presence expressed by the Greek word parousia—remains imminent. It is enough—or it would be enough—for human beings to see with eyes other than those of the flesh, and at last to learn how to look upon what is looking at them ...
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00906

Kay Khosraw's disappearance from the visible world unfolds in three stages. (a) He receives a revelation from Heaven calling on him to prepare for the “Great Renunciation.” He lives in meditation and prayer; his knights can no longer gain access to him. They become anxious. Have they offended him? When Zâl speaks to the king on their behalf, and they hear him speak of his approaching “ascent to Heaven,” they are terrified.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00907

Has their prince fallen prey to the same dizzy madness as his grandfather Kay Kâûs, who bound his throne to flying eagles and tried to force his way into the secrets of the starry heaven? But no: one cannot storm heaven's entrance with material machines. Their prince calms them with modest, measured words. (b) Kay Khosraw sets up camp outside the city. He solemnly confirms each of his warriors in his office and rank, then appoints Lohrasp as his successor, the founder of a new dynasty. (c) Kay Khosraw sets out for a high mountain.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00908

At first a lamenting crowd follows him. Eight of his knights decide to accompany him on the long journey, but their prince warns them: the path ahead leads through lands without water or vegetation; since they cannot follow him “as far as Heaven,” they should at least spare themselves the hardship of returning. Three heed his advice—Godarz, Zâl, and Rostam. The other five persist much longer, at the cost of great exhaustion.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00909

One evening they halt beside a spring. We are undoubtedly at the mysterious boundary, the Source of Life. Kay Khosraw tells his knights that they will never see him again. He gives them a final, solemn warning: a snowstorm is about to break; they must hurry back, or they will no longer find the way to this world. He then bathes in the spring, and suddenly his companions realize that he is no longer visible.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00910

Instead of following his advice, they search for him a long time, but cannot find him—just as the followers of the “Friend of God from the Highlands” will fail to find their master (see below, Book VII). They camp by the spring, talking of their vanished prince. Overcome with exhaustion, they fall asleep, and the storm buries them under deep drifts of snow.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00911

Thus their souls follow their lord, who has gone before them—though he himself did not have to cross the threshold of death—to the mystical castle of Kang-Dêz. He had already withdrawn there in meditation before announcing his “Great Renunciation” to his people.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00912

This, then, was the traditional image of Kay Khosraw that Suhrawardi had in mind when, in his Oriental Theosophy, he gave the prince so high a place among the sages of ancient Persia, and when he made him the subject of his own “Tale of the Grail.” Iran's heroic epic reaches its completion in mystical vision. The mystical epic succeeds the heroic epic, just as in Suhrawardi's writing the mystical tale takes the place of theoretical doctrinal exposition.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00913

As we have seen, Mr Coyajee established his comparison at the beginning of the heroic story, setting “The Childhood of Kay Khosraw” beside “The Childhood of Parsifal.” When that story reaches its fulfilment as a mystical epic, the task of comparative phenomenology seems to grow wider. The theme of concealment becomes especially important, because the mystery of that concealment can be considered at several levels.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00914

We may note, for our part, that in one continuation of Chrétien de Troyes—the Continuation of Manessier—Parsifal reigns for seven years, then retires to a hermitage and becomes a priest. “The Grail was with him night and day.” After his funeral, the Wondrous Objects—the Grail, the Lance, and the Silver Dish—appear upon his tomb. Then they vanish, and are never seen again. Here the Wondrous Objects become hidden from this world in the same way as the Xvarnah.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00915

But Parsifal himself disappears from this world by crossing the threshold of death, since the story tells us of his funeral. In the Queste del Saint-Graal, Parsifal is buried with Galahad in the “Spiritual Palace” of the mystical city of Sarras. Here we come closer to mystical concealment: to be buried in Sarras, and especially in its “Spiritual Palace,” is not to be buried in a city of this world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00916

Finally, in the Titurel of Albrecht von Scharfenberg, Parsifal and his knights carry the Holy Grail “to India,” and no one has seen them since. This time we encounter a form of the concealment of the Grail and its king that corresponds to the concealment of the Xvarnah and Kay Khosraw.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00917

Yet there seems to be another direction in which to look for these parallels: the correspondence between Kay Khosraw and King Arthur in their respective concealments and in the roles they will play at the end of time. We might compare Kang-Dêz, the mystical castle to which Kay Khosraw withdraws, with the enchanted island of Avalon (or Avallon) in Celtic tradition, that marvellous island of the Otherworld. It is an island bearing the fruits of immortality (Avalon, Avallach: the fruit that preserves from death); a mysterious, blessed island also called Insula puellarum, the Island of Maidens.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00918

We may note in passing that exactly the same name appears in certain Iranian traditions of the last things: shahr-e dokhtaran, the City of Maidens. Parsifal himself seems to pass through it during his Quest (the “Castle of Maidens” in the Continuation of Wauchier).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00919

But the enchanted castle or island of the Otherworld is always represented as a fortified, inaccessible place, invisible except to one who is invited, called, or chosen. It lies beyond the seas. Compare the voyage described in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Western Exile, or the journey to the Green Island, home of the Hidden Imam.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00920

We can therefore better understand why it is Water, in its supernatural state as the Source of Life, that hides Kay Khosraw from his companions after their last sight of him in this world. Similarly, after the Celts' final battle against the Saxon invader, King Arthur is mysteriously carried away to the island beyond the seas, the island of eternal youth. There his wounds are healed by the Regia Virgo, the island's queen—Morgan—whose beauty exceeds that of her divine companions.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00921

Hidden from the inhabitants of this world, Arthur will return to help his people and lead them to victory. In the same way, Kay Khosraw, having passed through the Water of Life, now dwells unseen in Kang-Dêz among the other companions of the hero of the last days. With that hero he will appear again on the Last Day to bring about the Transfiguration of the world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00922

We could draw on other traditions here, were our purpose not simply to suggest the convergence of certain Celtic and Zoroastrian traditions concerning the end of time. Judged by our ordinary measures of time and space, the last things seem to lie at the end of a long delay, at an immeasurable distance.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00923

But judged by their own time—as believers who live in the expectation of them experience them here and now, in their own Malakût—both delay and distance disappear. This fulfilment takes place with each mystical believer, as Suhrawardi's “Tale of the Grail” suggests. It transforms geographical places, whose sacred quality is then perceived by a faculty other than the senses. In the twelfth century, Avalon could be identified with the haunted ground on which Glastonbury Abbey was built.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00924

The same phenomenon occurs when the Grail castle is located at Montserrat, Montségur, or elsewhere, or when the site of Zoroaster's visions shifts from eastern Iran to western Iran, in the mountains of Azerbaijan. All these locations can be true, and true at the same time, because theirs is a different kind of truth from the one established by officials drawing up a land register.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00925

Everywhere and always, this truth involves the “symbolism of the centre,” and what William Blake, a visionary of the highest order, knew how to express: “And if a man changes his dwelling, his heavens accompany him—wherever he goes, and all his neighbours mourn his loss. Such are the spaces called earth, and such are their dimensions.” The Imago Terrae, the image of the earth, does nothing but reflect the Imago Animae, the image of the soul.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00926

And the Imago is neither an organ nor a representation that depends on empirical perceptions; on the contrary, it precedes, orders, and governs those perceptions. That is why it cannot convey its “object” to those who are indifferent, convince them of the holiness it perceives in certain places, or show them the bonds it perceives among certain events and persons. For it is the organ through which the Malakût is perceived.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00927

And this is precisely the phenomenon that a fully developed phenomenology has the task of “saving”—of safeguarding and making intelligible. It belongs to the same whole traced by the lineage of spiritual knowledge (silsilat al-’irfân) which Suhrawardi sees joining the Khosrawâniyûn to the Ishrâqîyûn when he draws the diagram of his spiritual ancestry. To allow a spiritual fact to reveal itself to us as it reveals itself to Suhrawardi is, at the same time, to understand the faith that gives rise to that fact—the intentional direction of that faith—and the horizons of meaning which the spiritual fact, in turn, makes possible and explains.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00928

Then Kay Khosraw's mystical castle, Kang-Dêz-behesht (Kang-Dêz Paradise), rises before us in the “eighth clime,” the same world to which the mystical city of Hûrqalyâ belongs: the “intermediate Orient.” Castle and city alike represent the “celestial pole,” in medio mundi, at the world's centre. They stand at the threshold of what Suhrawardi calls the “Orient of Lights,” the sources of the Xvarnah, where, in an eternal dawn, arise the divine manifestations contemplated by the sages of ancient Persia.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00929

The fact that Suhrawardi's mystical tales bring the heroic epic to completion as a mystical epic implies that the hero's deeds must be oriented from the beginning: they must tend toward this “Orient,” toward their fulfilment there. This “orientation” is the Oriental goal of the mystical epic. To reach that “Orient” is to give the epic and its heroes their eschatological meaning, their significance for what lies beyond this world and at the fulfilment of time.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00930

We may say that the mystical epic begins whenever the heroic epic—or the romantic or chivalric epic—is oriented in this way, in Suhrawardi's sense of “orient.” From that moment it has two poles, an “orient” and an “occident,” which is to say an inner meaning and an outer meaning, an esoteric and an exoteric dimension (bâtin and zâhir). This is a feature shared by the story of Kay Khosraw and the story of Parsifal.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00931

Whatever key opens up that meaning—Zoroastrianism, Hermeticism, Neoplatonism, or Celtic Christianity—it opens onto a horizon where the Malakût takes shape in concrete spiritual forms: the world where the soul's mystical castles stand. To reveal this meaning, the true meaning, is the work of spiritual interpretation, the ta’wîl whose supreme application in Shiism we have already examined.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00932

But we must not misunderstand. This does not mean simply reducing an imaginal event or a living vision to a few abstract theoretical propositions. That would be to turn our backs on the “Orient.” As we shall have occasion to say again, the event of the soul is itself—and is first of all—the ta’wîl that brings theoretical propositions back to the “Orient” in which they become true. This is the distinctive character of the hikâyat, the narrative that is at once history and imitation (mimesis). It is history because it imitates a higher world, and its imitation is the image (mithâl) of that world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00933

Here the power of images and imaginative perception to produce knowledge—their noetic function—becomes decisive. At the same time, the storyteller, the “historian,” can no longer be regarded as detached from the events narrated, without responsibility toward them. The listener or reader, for their part, can realize the meaning of those events only if this ta’wîl, this spiritual interpretation, takes place within them as well. The word ta’wîl itself carries the idea of a “passage,” a “turning back,” for it names the act of leading something back to its source, its archetype—its asl, its origin or “original.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00934
All those who have followed the spiritual paths of Islam have, of course, practised ta’wîl in interpreting the Quran.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00935

What is remarkable about Suhrawardi is that he knew how to apply ta’wîl to the figures of Iran's religious epic—not only Kay Khosraw, but others as well. For him, the deeds of the Iranian heroes, from the Avesta to the Shâh-Nâmeh, thus become part of the phenomenon of the Book that we examined earlier (Book I). Drawing on the interpretive resources offered by Islam's sacred Book, Suhrawardi rose to a vantage point from which he could bring within that same phenomenon of the Book the wisdom of ancient Persia's philosophers of divine things, the wisdom of Hermes, and that of the ancient Greeks and Neoplatonists.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00936
We cannot lightly judge—and still less dismiss, as has been done—Suhrawardi's attachment to Iran and its spiritual heritage.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00937
We must first understand that this Iranism is in no sense racial. It is hieratic, in the Neoplatonic sense of spiritual consecration which we have used here before.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00938

We must then understand the ta’wîl he practises, and confuse it neither with “allegory” nor with an arbitrary construction. Ta’wîl, spiritual interpretation, is not a dialectical construction. It discloses intentions and brings latent possibilities to life. It is the “unveiling of what is hidden” (kashf al-mahjûb). It can understand physical things theologically, which is quite different from “constructing” a physics.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00939

The Neoplatonists already understood this perfectly well. Ta’wîl leads an event back to its source, its “original”—that is, to the Malakût, to the event as it occurs, and as it has its place, in the Malakût. This is how Suhrawardi “leads back” the Iranian epic to its mystical meaning, to its Orient: he recognizes in it an epic already oriented toward that destination.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00940

Hence the importance that will be assumed by the mysterious bird Simorgh, a figure of the Holy Spirit. We see, then, that the Quest for the Orient reaches its fulfilment at the very point where the quests of Kay Khosraw and Parsifal reach theirs.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
en-book-2-ch-4-s4
4. The “Eastern” fulfilment of the heroic epic in the mystical epic
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00941

More generally, we should speak of a passage from epic or historical narrative to mystical narrative. The works in which Suhrawardi brings this passage to completion are short prose compositions, and this is precisely what sets them apart from the mystical epics that make up so important a part of Persian literature: the works of Attar, Jami, Assar of Tabriz, Khaju-yi Kermani, Katibi, and others. To bring together what has gone before, we shall try to prepare the way for understanding these mystical narratives—for their ta’wil, the interpretation that leads them back to their spiritual source—by considering two points.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00942

First, there is the idea of the “East” and of the “return to the East.” Here we can discern something shared by Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy, which fulfils the ishraqi project, and the Grail cycle discussed earlier, in which we detected affinities both with the spiritual world of ancient Persia and with Hermeticism. The Iranian spiritual heritage and Hermeticism are both living presences in Suhrawardi’s work; meanwhile, the adventure of the Grail ends in a “return to the East,” understood as a withdrawal from the sight of this world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00943

Second, there comes a moment when doctrine becomes an event of the soul. This is the decisive moment in which mystical narrative—Suhrawardi’s hikayat—takes shape, and we must understand both the transition and its true interpretation. In the Grail cycle as in Suhrawardi’s, the “Eastern” destiny gives the whole narrated adventure its direction and meaning.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00944

Kang-Dez is the mystical castle at the summit of Mount Qaf, where the adventure of Kay Khosraw comes to its end. Mount Qaf, as we know, is the world of the soul, the malakut, the “eighth clime.” The ishraqi tradition names several cities there, the “emerald cities,” with Hurqalya at their summit. The cycle of the Holy Grail likewise knows of a city “in the East,” where the Grail’s adventure ends: a place higher even than all the heights (Montserrat, Monsalvat, Montsegur) and mystical sites (Corbenic) where the Grail was revealed to its chosen ones in this world. That city is called Sarras. The name may evoke Sarracena, the country from which the Saracens were said to come, and the texts may place it “on the borders of Egypt”; but it would be as futile to search for its geographical coordinates on our maps as to search there for Hurqalya or the Green Island. “On the borders of Egypt” must be understood in the light of the tradition inherited by Suhrawardi, in which the biblical departure from Egypt is interpreted by ta’wil as departure from the “land of exile.” Indeed, Sarras has exactly the significance of the cities of the “eighth clime”: it is an “intermediate East,” a threshold between this world and the other. The Holy Grail rests there twice: first, when it is brought from the mystical Jerusalem to the West (Great Britain); and then, on its return to the East. There, once it crosses the threshold, it vanishes from human sight. These two journeys of the Grail correspond to the two movements familiar throughout Islamic theosophical gnosis: the soul’s descent and its return ascent (nozul and so’ud).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00945

On its “descent,” then, the Grail is carried by Joseph of Arimathea, his son Josephes, and their companions, who stop at Sarras. This has occasioned surprise, since the inhabitants are described as “pagans,” worshippers of the stars (like the Hermetic Sabians of Harran).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00946

But Sarras is precisely where we find ourselves in the malakut, the world of the Soul; and that world contains souls in all their diversity, with their many dwelling places. It is there that the soul’s battles take place. The key to Sarras is the palace described as the “Spiritual Palace” (Palais espiriteus), where the passage from the lower malakut to the higher malakut takes place.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00947

In this hidden world of the Soul, Joseph gives his first preaching. And in the sanctuary of the Spiritual Palace, his son Josephes is consecrated—with holy oil brought by angels—as the first Christian bishop and the first guardian of the Grail. He stands at the origin of a lineage which, as we have already seen, neither competes nor can even be compared with any worldly dynasty or canonically established succession. It knows nothing of such successions, for its “history” takes place elsewhere.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00948

Sarras appears again on the road of “return,” when Galahad, the high prince of “celestial” knighthood, brings the Grail adventure to completion. Having healed the wounded king at Corbenic, he sets out for Sarras in the “Holy Land,” accompanied by Percival and Bors. There Josephes appears once more, although he departed this earth long ago.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00949

But that is precisely the point: we are at Sarras now, no longer on this earth. We then hear the account of the Grail’s last Supper, in which, some centuries ago, the knighthood of the West perhaps entrusted its final secret. Surrounded by angels, Josephes celebrates the Grail liturgy in the Spiritual Palace of Sarras. He gives communion to Galahad; then, lifting the paten that covers the Grail, he invites the celestial knight to contemplate its mysteries. Galahad dies in ecstasy, and angels carry away his soul. A heavenly hand, attached to no visible body, seizes the Grail and the Lance and carries them “into heaven.” Never again are they seen in this world. Never again is the supernatural Mass of the Grail celebrated, nor the secret words of consecration spoken that Christ had entrusted to Joseph of Arimathea.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00950

From then on, the lineage of the Grail’s guardians is hidden from this world, and with it the whole knighthood of the Grail Templars. Similarly, with the Twelfth Imam, the line of Imams—the esoteric continuation of prophecy—entered into concealment; and with the concealment of the spiritual “pole,” the entire mystical hierarchy of his Friends and faithful followers also became hidden from human sight.
